items.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: send in Walter Booker and a lot of other guys who also enjoyed the experience that I was having working with this group of guys.

ctx.x: Yeah. I can hear and I know that that bass is important. We need, bass players are very important. But I didn’t want to change, he didn’t play, he played the pump and he was always playing the bass note. But I didn’t mind. I could hear what he was doing, and as long as I could hear it, you know, I said look, why disturb what he was doing? It’s okay. If we play the same note it’s okay. I don’t mind that. But it’s going to feel good. I’m going to make the note that he played, it’s going to feel so good to him. He’s…

send in Walter Booker and a lot of other guys who also enjoyed the experience that I was having working with this group of guys. I would do this during the day and at night I was working with Billy Taylor. So I got the chance to enjoy all of it. I had my cake and I ate it too.

Oh, that’s great. That’s about as good as it gets for a musician. I want to ask you to elaborate on one thing here for us. You, I’ve heard you, through our conversation so far, again and again talk about the feel of music. And then you talked about having fun with the music and laughing and the grooves that you get into. Kind of give us your take on why those things are so essential to jazz. Not that orchestral music or chamber music doesn’t have a given energy. But talk to us from the jazz standpoint of why…
